title: CyberPowerPC vs iBuyPower: Which Prebuilt Brand Is Better?
description: Neither wins outright: both use retail GPUs, 3-year labor warranties and similar prices. The better buy is the listing with the better PSU, RAM and price.
dek: How the two biggest prebuilt brands compare on parts, warranty, customization, price and support, plus where Skytech fits in.
quickAnswer: CyberPowerPC and iBuyPower are close to even. Both use retail graphics cards and CPUs, both have typically advertised three years of labor and one year of parts warranty with lifetime support, and both sell through the same stores at similar prices. Pick whichever listing has the better configuration at your price: a named power supply, two RAM sticks and a 1 TB SSD matter more than the logo.
intro: CyberPowerPC and iBuyPower are the two prebuilt brands people compare most, and their PCs often sit side by side at Best Buy, Amazon and Walmart. The differences are smaller than the brand loyalty online suggests.

This comparison uses each brand's listed parts, published warranty terms at the time of writing and the broad pattern of buyer reports. We have not bench-tested either brand's systems; performance comes from the GPU and CPU, which are the same retail parts in both.

sections.h: CyberPowerPC vs iBuyPower at a Glance
body: On paper the two brands are mirror images. The table summarizes the points that differ most in practice; warranty terms are as each brand published them at the time of writing and can change, so check the current page and the listing you buy from.

sections.h: Which Has Better Parts, CyberPowerPC or iBuyPower?
body: Neither, as a brand. Both put retail graphics cards and CPUs in every PC, so an [RTX 5070](/gear/rtx-5070/) in a CyberPowerPC and one in an iBuyPower run games at the same frame rate within normal variance. The parts that differ are the supporting ones, and they differ more between listings of the same brand than between brands.

Check the power supply (named brand and 80 Plus rating, enough wattage for the GPU per our [PSU calculator](/tools/psu-calculator/)), the RAM (two sticks for dual channel), the SSD (1 TB NVMe on a $900+ PC) and the CPU cooler. The listing that names all four is usually the better build.

They are effectively tied. Both have typically advertised a limited warranty of three years of labor and one year of parts, plus lifetime tech support, on systems bought directly, per their warranty pages at the time of writing. Retail-store systems from either brand may carry different terms, so read the warranty on the listing.

In practice, component warranties often outlast the system's parts term: graphics card makers commonly offer three years, and good power supplies and SSDs offer three to ten. That backup coverage is the same whichever brand assembled the PC.

Prices swing week to week with sales, and the same GPU tier usually lands within $50 to $100 across the two brands. The fair comparison is price against the parts list: add up the GPU, CPU, RAM, SSD, PSU and Windows, and the better deal is the system priced closest to that total with the better supporting parts. Our [how much does a gaming PC cost](/how-much-does-a-gaming-pc-cost/) guide shows the expected price of each tier.

Both offer configurators on their own websites where you can choose the case, GPU, CPU, RAM, storage and power supply. This is the best way to avoid the weak points of fixed retail configurations: you can pick a named Gold power supply, two RAM sticks and a larger SSD. Custom orders take longer to build and ship than in-stock retail units, which is the most common complaint about both brands.

Buyer reports for both describe the same pattern: support that resolves problems but can be slow during busy seasons. If fast help matters to you, buying from a retailer with an easy return window, such as Best Buy or Amazon, gives you a simpler route for early problems than either brand's RMA process.

sections.h: Which Brand Is Better at Each Budget?
body: At the budget end, around $700 to $1,000, both brands sell RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT class systems, and this is where corner-cutting is most common. Single-stick RAM, 500 GB SSDs and unnamed power supplies show up most often here, from both brands. The best budget listing is the one that avoids all three, even if it costs $30 to $50 more. Our [best budget gaming PC](/best-budget-gaming-pc/) and [best gaming PC under $1,000](/best-gaming-pc-under-1000/) pages compare current options.

In the mid-range, $1,200 to $1,600, both brands usually step up to named Gold power supplies, two RAM sticks and 1 TB SSDs around an RTX 5070 or RX 9070. This is the price band where the two are hardest to separate, and where a sale price decides it.

At the high end, $1,800 and above with an RTX 5070 Ti or RTX 5080, both use liquid coolers and showcase cases. Check that the power supply is 850 W or more for an RTX 5080, and that the case has enough intake fans; glass-fronted cases can run warm. At this price it is also worth comparing a custom configuration on each brand's site, which lets you pick the exact power supply and cooler.

sections.h: How Do Their Cases and Upgrade Paths Compare?
body: Both brands use standard ATX and micro-ATX motherboards, power supplies and cases in most systems, so RAM, storage and graphics card upgrades work the same way as on a home-built PC. Before adding a bigger GPU later, check the power supply's wattage and connectors, and the case's maximum GPU length, which listings often omit but the case maker publishes.

Case designs are where the brands look most different. Both lean on tempered-glass showcase cases with RGB fans; iBuyPower's Y40 and Y60 and CyberPowerPC's Gamer Supreme are popular examples. Mesh-front cases run cooler and quieter under load, so if you don't care about the look, a mesh-front listing is the better choice at the same price.

Skytech is the third brand in most comparisons. It uses the same kind of retail GPUs and CPUs, sells mainly on Amazon and often has the most attractive cases at a given price, but it has typically published a shorter labor warranty than CyberPowerPC and iBuyPower. Our [Skytech gaming PC review](/skytech-gaming-pc-review/) covers it in detail.

Buy the listing, not the brand. If a CyberPowerPC and an iBuyPower have the same GPU and price, choose the one with the named power supply, dual-channel RAM and bigger SSD. If both are equal, choose the store with the better return window. For full brand reviews, see [is CyberPowerPC good](/is-cyberpowerpc-good/) and [is iBuyPower good](/is-ibuypower-good/), and for current picks, our [best prebuilt gaming PC](/best-prebuilt-gaming-pc/) roundup.

mistakes: Online loyalty for one brand rarely reflects a real difference. Two listings from the same brand can differ more than the two brands do.
A cheaper PC with a slower graphics card isn't a better deal. Compare systems with the same GPU, then look at the supporting parts and price.
Early problems are easiest to solve by returning to the store. Prefer the retailer with the longer, simpler return policy when prices are equal.
Assuming retail and direct warranties match
Store-bought units can carry different terms. Read the warranty on the exact listing.
If no fixed configuration has a named PSU and two RAM sticks, a custom order from either brand usually fixes that for a small extra cost.
bottomLine: CyberPowerPC and iBuyPower are near-identical choices: both build with retail GPUs and CPUs, both have typically advertised three years of labor and one year of parts warranty, and both sell at similar prices through the same stores. Compare exact listings: the one with a named power supply, two RAM sticks and a 1 TB SSD at the lower price is the better buy, whichever logo it carries.

faqs.a: Neither is better overall. They use the same kinds of parts and similar warranties. The better buy is whichever listing has the stronger power supply, RAM and SSD at your price.
Not consistently. The same GPU tier usually costs within $50 to $100 across the two, and sales change which is cheaper week to week.

faqs.q: Which has the better warranty, CyberPowerPC or iBuyPower?
faqs.a: They are similar: both have typically advertised three years of labor and one year of parts, plus lifetime support, per their warranty pages at the time of writing. Check current terms.

faqs.q: Is Skytech better than CyberPowerPC or iBuyPower?
faqs.a: Skytech is comparable on parts and price and often has nicer cases for the money, but it has typically published a shorter labor warranty than both. Compare the exact configurations and warranty terms of the listings you are considering.

faqs.q: Do CyberPowerPC and iBuyPower use cheap parts?
faqs.a: Their GPUs and CPUs are retail parts. Budget listings from both can use unnamed power supplies and single-stick RAM, so check those before buying.

faqs.q: Which is better for custom builds?
faqs.a: Both offer configurators on their websites. Use them to choose a named PSU and dual-channel RAM; custom orders take longer to ship.

faqs.q: Can I buy either brand at Best Buy?
faqs.a: Yes, both sell fixed configurations at Best Buy. See our Best Buy prebuilt gaming PC guide for what to check in-store.

faqs.q: Are CyberPowerPC and iBuyPower good for gaming?
faqs.a: Yes. Performance comes from the graphics card, so pick an RTX 5060 class card for 1080p, an RTX 5070 or RX 9070 for 1440p and an RTX 5070 Ti or faster for 4K.
